title: CSRF & Request Forgery
summary: Cookies authenticate a browser, not an intent — CSRF exploits that gap to make a victim's browser send requests they never meant to. Covers the synchronizer token, double-submit cookie, and SameSite defenses.

slides.markdown:
[XSS](xss) exploits a browser rendering untrusted script. **CSRF** exploits something more subtle: a browser automatically attaching your credentials to *any* request to a site you're logged into, regardless of which page told it to send that request.

That automatic attachment — a cookie sent with every request to its domain — is exactly what makes session auth convenient. It's also exactly what a malicious page can abuse: trick your browser into firing a request to your bank, your email, or your admin panel, and your browser helpfully attaches your session cookie, no questions asked.

This topic covers why that happens, the two classic token-based defenses, and the modern `SameSite` cookie attribute that closes most of it at the browser level with zero application code.

**Cross-Site Request Forgery** tricks a victim's browser into sending a request to a site it's already authenticated for, from a page the victim didn't intend to trigger that request from.

Say `bank.com` lets you transfer money via `POST /transfer` using only your session cookie to authenticate. A malicious page at `evil.com` includes a hidden auto-submitting form that also posts to `bank.com/transfer` with the attacker's account as the destination. If you're logged into `bank.com` and you visit `evil.com` — maybe via a link in an email — your browser submits that form and **attaches your `bank.com` session cookie automatically**, because that's just what browsers do for same-domain cookies, regardless of which page triggered the request.

`bank.com`'s server sees a perfectly well-formed, authenticated request. It has no way to tell that the *intent* behind it came from an attacker's page rather than the bank's own transfer form.

The security-theory name for the root cause is **ambient authority**: a cookie proves *who you are* to the server, but it proves nothing about *what you intended to do right now*. It's attached automatically, silently, to every request — the browser doesn't ask "does the current page actually want to send this on the user's behalf."

Compare this to something like a bank PIN entered at an ATM: the PIN is deliberate, tied to this specific transaction, and only you can supply it at this moment. A session cookie is the opposite — persistent, automatic, and reusable by *any* page that can get your browser to fire a request, for as long as the session lasts.

This is why the fix categories below don't touch authentication at all — you're already correctly authenticated when a CSRF attack succeeds. The fix has to add a *second* signal that specifically proves the current page's intent, since the cookie alone can never carry that information.

The classic, most robust defense: the server generates a **unique, unpredictable token per session (or per form)**, embeds it in a hidden field on the legitimate form, and requires that exact token to be resubmitted with the request.

```html
<form method="POST" action="/transfer">
  <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="a1b2c3...">
  <!-- other fields -->
</form>
```

The server checks the submitted `csrf_token` against the one it issued for that session. `evil.com` can make your browser send a request to `bank.com/transfer` with your cookie attached automatically — but it has **no way to read** the token value, because that value lives in `bank.com`'s own HTML, which `evil.com` cannot access thanks to the browser's same-origin policy. No token, no valid request.

The token proves the request originated from a page that could actually read the legitimate form — exactly the intent signal a cookie alone can't provide.

A lighter-weight alternative that avoids server-side session storage for the token: the server sets a random token as a **cookie**, and client-side JavaScript reads that cookie and includes its value as a request header or hidden field. The server then checks that the header/field value matches the cookie value.

Why this still works against CSRF: `evil.com` can make your browser send a request with your `bank.com` cookies attached, but it **cannot read** `bank.com`'s cookie value to put it in a matching header — same-origin policy blocks that. So even though the cookie itself travels automatically, the attacker can't produce the matching header value the check requires.

The trade-off versus the synchronizer token: no server-side storage needed (stateless, easier to scale), but it's weaker against an attacker who can set cookies on your domain at all — for example via a subdomain takeover or an XSS bug elsewhere on the same site — so it's often paired with other defenses rather than used alone.

`SameSite` is a browser-enforced cookie attribute that tells the browser **when** to attach a cookie to a cross-site request, closing most CSRF at the browser level with no application code at all. - **`SameSite=Strict`** — the cookie is never sent on a cross-site request, full stop, even when a user clicks a legitimate link from another site into yours. Maximally safe, but breaks the "click a link from an email and land already logged in" experience. - **`SameSite=Lax`** — the cookie is sent on top-level navigation (clicking a link) but withheld from cross-site subrequests like a form auto-submit, an `` tag, or a background `fetch`/`XHR` — which covers the classic CSRF pattern while preserving normal link-clicking UX. This is the modern browser default when no attribute is set. - **`SameSite=None`** — the cookie is sent on every cross-site request, matching legacy behavior; requires the `Secure` attribute (HTTPS only) alongside it. `Lax` alone stops the hidden-auto-submitting-form attack from the earlier example, since that's a cross-site subrequest, not a top-level navigation. It's a major mitigation but not a total substitute for tokens, covered next.

slides.sectionTitle: A CSRF attack, step by step
slides.markdown:
![A hidden auto-submitting form on evil.com triggers a request to bank.com with the victim's session cookie attached automatically](assets/csrf-cross-site-request.svg)

The diagram makes the core confusion visible: the request really is authenticated — that part is genuine. What's forged is the *intent* behind it. Every defense in this topic is really answering the same question: how does the server tell a genuine, victim-intended request apart from a genuine-looking, attacker-triggered one, when the cookie alone says nothing about intent.

slides.sectionTitle: CSRF vs XSS: different problem, often confused
slides.markdown:
| | CSRF | XSS |
|---|---|---|
| **What's exploited** | The browser's automatic cookie attachment | The browser executing untrusted script |
| **Attacker needs** | The victim to load a malicious page, no script injection needed | To inject script into the target site itself |
| **Where the payload runs** | On the attacker's own page (`evil.com`) | On the target site's own page |
| **What it can do** | Trigger one specific request the attacker crafted in advance | Anything JavaScript can do — read cookies, make arbitrary requests, modify the page |
| **Primary fix** | CSRF tokens, `SameSite` cookies | Output encoding, CSP |

The frequent confusion: **XSS can be used to defeat CSRF defenses**, because injected script running on the target site can read the CSRF token directly out of the page and submit it — so a CSRF token doesn't protect you if the site also has an XSS bug. They're separate vulnerabilities, but XSS strictly dominates CSRF in capability once it lands: an attacker with XSS on your site rarely needs CSRF at all.

A persistent misconception: HTTPS protects request contents in transit, so surely it stops CSRF too.

It doesn't, and the reason clarifies what HTTPS actually does versus what CSRF exploits:

- **HTTPS protects confidentiality and integrity in transit** — it stops an on-path attacker from reading or tampering with a request as it travels over the network.
- **CSRF happens entirely inside a legitimate, correctly-encrypted request.** The victim's browser genuinely does send an authentic, HTTPS-protected request to `bank.com`, with a valid session cookie, over a secure channel. Nothing about the request is tampered with in transit — it's forged at the *origin*, on the attacker's page, before encryption even applies.
- **The attacker never needs to intercept anything.** They just need the victim's browser to visit a page they control, which HTTPS on the target site does nothing to prevent.

HTTPS and CSRF defenses solve different problems entirely: one is about the channel, the other is about whether the request itself represents genuine user intent.

slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown: A junior answer to "how do you prevent CSRF" picks one defense. A senior answer layers them, because each has a gap the others cover: - **`SameSite=Lax` as the baseline**, since it's free (a cookie attribute, no code) and stops the majority of classic CSRF with zero developer effort — most modern frameworks and browsers default to it already. - **CSRF tokens for state-changing requests specifically**, as defense-in-depth for the cases `SameSite` doesn't fully cover — some legitimate top-level navigations, certain older browsers, or subdomain-adjacent trust boundaries. - **Recognizing that GET requests should never mutate state.** A surprising amount of "CSRF-proof" advice quietly assumes this. If `GET /transfer?to=attacker&amount=1000` actually performs a transfer, it's forgeable via a plain `` tag with no form and no JavaScript at all — the fix there isn't a CSRF token, it's fixing the API to not mutate state on GET. - **Treating any XSS finding as a CSRF-defense bypass**, since injected script can read tokens directly. A CSRF token audit is incomplete without an XSS audit alongside it. The unifying instinct: no single control is complete, and knowing *which* gap each layer closes is what separates reciting "use a CSRF token" from actually closing the class.
